The "Candle Maker's Petition" is a satire of protectionist tariffs written the by great French economist, Frederic Bastiat. In many ways, it expanded on the free market argument against mercantilism set forth by Adam Smith, but Bastiat's target was government tariffs that were levied to protect domestic industries from competition. In Bastiat's "Candle Maker's Petition", all the people involved in the French lighting industry, including "the manufacturers of candles, tapers, lanterns, sticks, street lamps, snuffers and extinguishers, and from producers of tallow, oil, resin, alcohol, and generally of everything connected with lighting" call upon the French government to take protective action against the unfair competition of the sun.

They argue that forcing people to close "all windows, dormers, skylights, inside and outside shutters, curtains, casements, bull's-eyes, deadlights, and blinds - in short, all openings, holes, chinks, and fissures through which the light of the sun is wont to enter houses" will lead to a higher consumption of candles and related products. In turn, they reason, the industries that those in the lighting industry depend on for materials will have greater sales, as will their dependent suppliers, and so on until everyone is better off without the sun.

This satirical essay suggests that forcing people to pay for something when a free alternative is available is often a waste of resources. In this case, the money that people spend on additional lighting products would indeed boost profit for candle makers, but because this expenditure is not required, it is wasteful, and diverts money from other products.

The thing is protectionism is a good way to hedge against sanctions and war. Is it good that Europe relies on Russia for natural gas? Would the Iranians not be able to pursue their nuclear program in peace if it weren't for the massive bevy of sanctions placed upon them? Is it not true that a large reason for Japan attacking America during world war II was that America had recently cut Japan off from its oil?

When a nation must rely on other nations for even the most basic of goods it is an inherent infringement upon its national sovereignty.

'National sovereignty' is only as good as the policies and behavior of the ruling party of the nation which it insulates. It's not necessarily something worthy of universal maximization in the absence of particulars.

I think a stronger argument for tariffs would be to describe it as a mechanism for capturing externalities related to foreign corruption and exploitation.

For instance, suppose a 'North Korea'-like state decided to use political prisoners as slave labor to cheaply manufacture commodities. What a democratic country could due to exert pressure to end these practices, is tying a large scaling import tariff on all goods from North Korea, in order to create a profit incentive for anyone in North Korea who could make money from export to internally pressure the state into reducing anti-democratic policies and treating its citizens better.

Basically, if you use automatically scaling import tariff rates tied to a public criteria of human rights abuses \ value incompatabilities, so you have close to a 0% rate between aligned democracies enabling quicker economic development and trade benefits, and possibly a 50-1000% tariff against the monarchies and dictatorships depending on level of atrocities. Having an internationally known scaling rule could create a profit incentive to improve behavior on the margin and possibly decrease the likelihood of sanctions\war occurring in the first place.
